info.text: In this demo we'll learn how to create a basic front end for an LLM (large language model) running in the "cloud", by which I mean a data center owned and operated by another company.
info.title: getting started
libraries
info.text: First I've loaded a couple of libraries, my netnet-standard-library (or nn for short) as well as an extention called nn.prompt, which is a function we'll use to send messages to LLMs hosted elsewhere.

info.title: global variables
info.text: The first thing we'll include in our code is a few global variables, PROVIDER which will store the name of the LLM provider we want to use, MODEL which is the name of the specific LLM we want to use and then three more which will become references to elements we'll create in our first function.

info.title: setup function
info.text: Our sketch has three functions, the first is our setup function which we'll be using to create all the HTML UI (user interface) elements on our page.

info.title: load event
info.text: The last line in our demo, which runs after we've defined all our functions, is an event listener which is going to run our setup function as soon as the page loads.

info.title: API key input field
info.text: The first thing our setup function creates is an input field for the user to place their API key. Cloud-based LLM providers require that you create an account on their platform in order to generate an API key. These usually require up-front payment, but Google's Gemini does provide a free tier.

info.title: front-end vs back-end
info.text: When integrating a third-party provider's LLM into your own app like this, it is possible to store your own API key on your sever, in which case you'd be paying for everyone who uses your app. In this demo, we're keeping everything client-side or "front end", we're not writing any code or storing any data server-side on the "back end".

info.title: user keys
info.text: Because it's not safe to include private API keys in your font-end code (because it is visible to anyone who views your source), our sketch asks the user to insert their own key. This has the added benefit of not having to pay for all your user's queries, anyone using your app is responsible for registering their own key.

info.title: key input event
info.text: Notice that the input element we created also has its own event listener attached. It runs a function called storeKeyLocally anytime the user inputs text into the field.

info.title: key storing function
info.text: If we take a look at the storeKeyLocally function defined below, you'll notice it contains a single line of code which takes the value currently stored in the keyInput element and stores it in the browser's localStorage under the arbitrary name "gemini-key".

info.title: load previously stored key
info.text: Back in our setup function, right after we create that input field we're checking to see if there's currently an item stored in the user's browser's local storage under the name "gemini-key". If so, we're automatically setting the input field's value to whatever they had previously input, this way they don't have to input their key each time they load our app. Otherwise, (that's what || means here) we'll default to an empty string '', meaning the field remains empty.

info.title: saftey and convenience
info.text: While it's not technically necessary to store the user's key locally in their browser, not having to insert their API key everytime they open your page makes for a more pleasant user experience. The browser's localStorage is also a safe place to put their key because only the user with access to this browser will be able to access it.

info.title: prompt input
info.text: Moving on, the next element this function creates is a br (or line break) before creating another input field, this time for the text prompt we want to send to the LLM.

info.title: send button
info.text: The last thing we create is a p element we call ouput, because it's where we're going to display the LLM's output when we receive it. Just before that though, we create a button which also has an event listener attached, this one runs a function called send as soon as the user clicks the button.

info.title: send function
info.text: Let's take a look at what that send function does. First, notice that this function is declared with the async keyword. That's because sending a request to a third-party API always takes some time to receive a reply, which means we need to await for that reply, making this an asynchronous function.

info.title: "thinking"
info.text: As soon as the user clicks "send" the first thing we do is display some feedback, we update our p element's content to display the text ...thinking..., this lets the user know that we've sent their prompt to the API and are awaiting a response.

info.title: nn.prompt
info.text: Immediately after, we run nn.prompt the special function we use to send a request to an LLM provider. We pass the name of the provider we're using, 'gemini', the model we want to run, 'gemini-3.5-flash-lite', the API key our user provided in the keyInput field as well as the message they wrote in the input text field.

info.title: await
info.text: Remember, because it takes time to receive the response from the provider's API, we have to place the await keyword before the function call.

info.title: reply object
info.text: Once the response is received, we'll store all the data the provider's API sent us back in a variable we've named reply. This variable now becomes an object with lots of data stored inside, you can inspect the full response sent back by logging reply.raw to your web console.

info.title: output text
info.text: That said, the only piece of data we care about for this demo is the text the LLM synthesized in response to our user's input message prompt, which we can access via the reply.text property. The last line of our send function uses that text to update our output element's content so the user can see the reply.

info.title: other providers
info.text: That's the core logic required for creating your own AI-UI. Keep in mind you can use other providers as well, each of which has their own list of models, including OpenAI and Anthropic.

info.title: local models
info.text: We chose Google, for this demo because their API provides a free tier. OpenAI and Anthropic both require a credit card to get started. But you don't have to use any of these providers, depending on your use case you could also run open models locally on your comptuer with an app like Ollama.

info.title: nn.prompt docs
info.text: To learn more about the nn.prompt function including how to use it to send requests to other providers and local models, check out its documentation page on the library's GitHub.
